## Setting up the right ceiling

The naive answer is tempting: Carnot between 565 °C (838 K) and ambient (~25 °C, 298 K) gives

η_Carnot = 1 − 298/838 ≈ **64%**

But that bound assumes heat is added *isothermally* at 565 °C — which is unphysical here. The hot salt is a finite-heat-capacity stream, not an infinite reservoir: it gives up its heat by cooling from 565 °C down to the cold-tank return temperature (~290 °C for solar salt, set by the salt's freezing point ~220 °C plus margin). No engine can hold the salt at 838 K while extracting all that heat — once the salt cools, so must the maximum temperature at which that increment of heat is delivered.

The correct second-law ceiling is the **exergy of a sensible-heat stream** cooling from T₁ to T₂ against a sink at T₀ — equivalent to a Rankine cycle with infinite regenerative feedwater heating ("Carnotized" heat addition, which exactly tracks the salt's cooling curve):

η_max = 1 − T₀·ln(T₁/T₂)/(T₁−T₂)

With T₁ = 838 K, T₂ = 563 K, T₀ = 298–313 K (25–40 °C):

**η_max ≈ 55–57%**

That ~7-8 point haircut versus naive Carnot isn't an engineering shortfall — it's the law-permitted ceiling once you respect that the heat source genuinely has a temperature glide. This is the honest number to benchmark against, not 64%.

## Where current practice sits

Molten-salt towers run live steam around ~540 °C (pinch/approach losses off the 565 °C bulk salt) at subcritical pressures (~100–165 bar) with single reheat — thermodynamically similar to a conventional subcritical coal reheat cycle. Deployed plants (Gemasolar, Crescent Dunes, Noor III-class) report **gross design-point cycle efficiencies of ~40–42%**, with annual net figures often 37–39% once parasitics and part-load/off-design operation are folded in.

**Gap: ~15 percentage points absolute (~27% relative) below the 55–57% ceiling.**

## Decomposing the gap — and what's recoverable

| Loss source | Rough size | Recoverable? |
|---|---|---|
| Boiler pinch mismatch — isothermal boiling against the glide-temperature salt stream (finite feedwater-heater stages, not infinite) | ~4–6 pts | Partially — supercritical steam pressure (removes the boiling plateau) and more FWH stages claw back ~2–3 pts, but CSP units are too small (20–150 MWe) for supercritical economics to pencil out easily |
| Turbine isentropic losses, LP-stage wetness (no moisture separator/reheat like nuclear plants use) | ~3–5 pts | Partially — better blading, extra reheat recovers ~1–2 pts |
| Condenser ITD above true ambient (air-cooled condensers, common in desert siting for water scarcity, run 50–60 °C vs. the 25 °C used in the ceiling calc) | ~2–4 pts | Partially — wet/hybrid cooling recovers most of this where water is available, but is often deliberately foregone |
| Pump/generator/mechanical losses | ~1 pt | Marginal — already 98–99% efficient components |
| Part-load/off-design operation (annual vs. design-point) | a few pts (shows up in the net/gross gap) | Largely already captured — this is exactly what the storage tanks are *for*, letting the turbine run near its design point more hours/year |

Summing the optimistic recoverable increments: **roughly 6–10 of the 15 points** could plausibly be clawed back with best-available steam-Rankine engineering (supercritical pressure, more feedwater-heater stages, improved turbine aerodynamics, wet cooling where feasible) — pushing practice from ~41% toward perhaps 48–50%.

The **remaining ~6–9 points is structurally locked in**, not by physics but by Rankine-cycle architecture and CSP plant economics: a finite (not infinite) number of feedwater heaters is a capex/efficiency trade-off, isothermal phase change is intrinsic to steam as a working fluid, and desert siting trades cooling performance for water availability. Closing that residual would require abandoning the steam Rankine cycle itself — e.g., supercritical-CO₂ Brayton or Kalina bottoming cycles — which is outside the scope of "the steam Rankine power block" as posed.

**Bottom line:** ceiling ≈ 56%, practice ≈ 41%, gap ≈ 15 points, of which roughly half is recoverable engineering headroom and roughly half is baked into the choice of steam as the working fluid at this plant scale.
